pearson.question: Is there a statistically significant linear relationship between Screen Time and Stress Score?
pearson.nullHypothesis: H₀: ρ = 0 (There is no true linear association between Screen Time and Stress Score in the student population).
pearson.altHypothesis: H₁: ρ ≠ 0 (A significant non-zero linear correlation exists between Screen Time and Stress Score).
pearson.decisionRule: Since p-value (0.001) < α (0.05), we reject H₀ and conclude that higher screen time is significantly correlated with higher stress.

assumptions.name: Linearity
assumptions.detail: Scatter plot confirms continuous monotonic linear trajectory

assumptions.name: Homoscedasticity
assumptions.detail: Equal variance across screen time intervals confirmed by Breusch-Pagan test

pearson.interpretation: A 1-hour increase in daily screen time is associated with an average 3.75 point increase in student stress score, explaining 17.6% of the variance.

chiSquare.question: Is Student Stress Level category significantly associated with Gender?
chiSquare.variableY: Stress Level (Low, Moderate, High, Very High)
chiSquare.nullHypothesis: H₀: Stress Level and Gender are independent in the student population.
chiSquare.altHypothesis: H₁: Stress Level and Gender are dependent (contingency distributions differ significantly).
chiSquare.decisionRule: Since p-value (0.016) < α (0.05), we reject H₀. There is a statistically significant association between gender and stress classification.

assumptions.name: Expected Frequencies
assumptions.detail: All expected contingency cell frequencies exceed 5 (Min cell E = 9.7)

assumptions.name: Mutual Exclusivity
assumptions.detail: Each observation is categorized into exactly one cell

chiSquare.interpretation: Female students exhibit a slightly higher proportion in High/Very High categories (42.5%) compared to Male students (35.8%), representing a statistically verifiable difference.

anova.question: Does average Stress Score significantly differ across University Types?
anova.nullHypothesis: H₀: μ_Public = μ_Private = μ_Research (The population mean stress scores are equal across all three institutional types).
anova.altHypothesis: H₁: At least one university type has a population mean stress score that differs from the others.
anova.decisionRule: Since p-value (0.007) < α (0.05), we reject H₀. Institutional structure has a statistically significant main effect on student stress.

assumptions.name: Normality within Groups
assumptions.detail: Q-Q plots confirm bell-shaped distribution per institutional group

assumptions.name: Homogeneity of Variances
assumptions.detail: Levene's Test p = 0.142 > 0.05 (equal variance assumption holds)

anova.interpretation: Post-hoc Tukey HSD reveals that Private University students experience significantly higher stress (mean = 67.1) compared to Public University students (mean = 62.4, p = 0.005).
